source_text: III. Advenientes vero parentes eius, videntes eum torqueri precabantur eum, hinc pueri pedes eius amplectentes dicebant: Miserere tui et nostri, pater; inde uxores lugentes vultum et aetatem eius precabantur. parentum vero omnium luctus et fletus erat super eum, domesticorum gemitus, vicinorum ululatus et lamentatio amicorum, qui omnes clamantes ad eum dicebant: Tenerae adolescentiae tuae miserere. sed, ut dictum est, meliore cupiditate detentus, sententiam domini ante oculos habens, quae dixit: Si quis me negaverit coram hominibus, et ego negabo eum coram patre meo qui in caelis est: omnes ergo despiciens nulli eorum respondit. festinabat enim ad supernae spem vocationis pervenire. Probus praeses dixit: Quid dicis? flectere horum lacrymis ab insania tua et consulens adolescentiae tuae sacrifica. Irenaeus respondit: Consulo mihi in perpetuum, si non sacrificavero. Probus iussit eum recipi in custodiam carceris. plurimis vero diebus ibidem clausus diversis poenis est affectus.
pass_a_gloss: His parents arriving and seeing him being twisted under torture kept begging him; on one side children embracing his feet said pity yourself and us, father, while on the other side mourning wives kept entreating him by his face and his age; there was mourning and weeping of all his kin over him, groaning of his household, howling of neighbors and lament of friends, all shouting to him pity your tender youth; but, as has been said, held fast by a better desire and holding before his eyes the sentence of the Lord who said if anyone denies me before men I too will deny him before my Father in heaven, he therefore looked down on them all and answered none of them, for he was hurrying to attain the hope of the calling from above; the governor Probus said what do you say, be bent by their tears away from your madness and take thought for your youth and sacrifice; Irenaeus answered I take thought for myself unto eternity if I do not sacrifice; Probus ordered him to be taken back into prison custody; shut up there for very many days he was afflicted with various punishments.
pass_b_english: Then his parents came, and when they saw him under torture they pleaded with him.
On one side the children clung to his feet and said, Pity yourself and us, father, and on the other side the grieving women entreated him by his countenance and his years.

Over him there lay the mourning and weeping of all his kin, the groans of his household, the wailing of his neighbors, and the lamentation of his friends, and they all cried out to him together, Pity your tender youth.

But, as it has been told, he was held fast by a better longing, and he kept before his eyes the sentence of the Lord, who said: If any man denies me before men, I also will deny him before my Father who is in heaven (Matthew 10:33).
Therefore he scorned them all and answered not one of them, for he was pressing on to lay hold of the hope of the calling from above.
The governor Probus said to him: What do you say?
Let their tears bend you from your madness, take thought for your youth, and sacrifice.
Irenaeus answered: I take thought for myself for eternity, if I do not sacrifice.
Probus ordered him to be taken back into the keeping of the prison, and shut up there for very many days he was worn down with divers pains.

choices.english: held fast by a better longing
choices.why: ablative of means with detentus, and cupiditas here is positive zeal toward heaven, contrasted with family affection, so longing fits better than lust

choices.term: Consulo mihi in perpetuum, si non sacrificavero
choices.english: I am taking thought for myself for eternity, if I do not sacrifice
choices.why: consulo with dative mihi means to take counsel for someone's interest, answering Probus's consulens with a deliberate echo, and future perfect protasis gives the condition for lasting safety

choices.english: the hope of the calling from above
choices.why: supernae agrees with vocationis as heavenly calling, and spes with genitive is the hoped-for object, not merely earthly hope
